## Atomic Factual Intents

### D0001 — Banxico accelerated monetary tightening to fight broad-based inflation
- **actor**: Banco de México (Banxico)
- **action**: responded to inflationary pressures with an acceleration in the pace of monetary tightening
- **mechanism**: initial 25 basis-point hikes, escalated to 50 bp, then 75 bp hikes once inflation became increasingly broad-based
- **outcome**: policy rate reached 9.25 percent, approximately 6 percentage points above the U.S. Fed rate; markets priced a terminal policy rate of about 10.5 percent by the first quarter of 2023
- **dates**: through mid-2022; terminal rate projected Q1 2023
- **quantities**: 25/50/75 bp hikes; 9.25% policy rate; ~6 pp differential vs Fed; 10.5% terminal priced
- **attribution**: IMF staff
- **period fit**: 2022 H1–early 2023 monetary stance
- **limitations**: pertains to Banxico, not direct fiscal authority of the executive; ruler attribution partial
- **polarity**: supportive of macroeconomic stabilization (positive for 5B.3)
- **methodology IDs**: 5B.3, 5B.9, 8B.2, 8B.5
- **source**: MAC-010
- **locator**: page 10
- **inclusive segments**: S00005–S00007

### D0002 — Peso yields/risk spreads rose while Mexico's spread widened less than peers
- **actor**: financial markets (peso bond markets, nonresident investors)
- **action**: interest rates and bond yields on peso-denominated debt rose to their highest levels since the Global Financial Crisis; one-year government bond yield rose over 250 bps; real Udibono 2031 yield rose 80 bps; foreign-currency Mexican sovereign spread widened less than most similar-credit sovereigns
- **mechanism**: response to Banxico rate hikes, diminished EM risk appetite, higher safe-asset yields
- **outcome**: tightened financial conditions; relative spread advantage vs peers
- **dates**: 2022 year-to-date
- **quantities**: 250+ bps on 1-year govt bond; 80 bps on Udibono 2031; 20-year bond yield increase mentioned
- **attribution**: IMF staff
- **period fit**: 2022 H1
- **limitations**: factual market data, not ruler action; ruler attribution indirect
- **polarity**: descriptive of stress (neutral for 5B; mild negative for stability, but spread performance positive)
- **methodology IDs**: 5B.7, 5B.9
- **source**: MAC-010
- **locator**: page 10
- **inclusive segments**: S00008–S00010

### D0003 — IMF Financial Conditions Index indicates moderate tightening, well below past peaks
- **actor**: IMF staff
- **action**: FCI for Mexico indicates a moderate increase by end-June 2022
- **mechanism**: indexed deviations from mean across multiple indicators
- **outcome**: level still well below past peaks
- **dates**: end-June 2022
- **quantities**: qualitative "moderate"
- **attribution**: IMF staff estimates
- **period fit**: mid-2022
- **limitations**: index-based, comparisons to historical peaks
- **polarity**: neutral description
- **methodology IDs**: 5B.7, 5B.9
- **source**: MAC-010
- **locator**: page 10
- **inclusive segments**: S00007–S00008

### D0004 — Peso remained broadly stable despite moderate portfolio outflows
- **actor**: portfolio investors (nonresidents); domestic institutional investors (notably pension funds)
- **action**: moderate portfolio outflows continued; nonresidents sold peso-denominated government bonds; offset by strong domestic institutional buying
- **mechanism**: offsetting flows; sales predated the pandemic and affected other large EM issuers
- **outcome**: peso remained stable against USD; supported by rising rate differential vs U.S., strong fiscal fundamentals, monetary policy commitment to price stability, and solid remittance inflows
- **dates**: past year through 2022 H1
- **quantities**: offsetting flows shown as chart (USD billions)
- **attribution**: Bank of Mexico, Ministry of Finance, IMF staff estimates
- **period fit**: 2021–2022 H1
- **limitations**: descriptive of market outcomes; ruler attribution indirect (Banxico/MP monetary framework)
- **polarity**: positive (stable currency, strong institutional offset)
- **methodology IDs**: 5B.3, 5B.9, 8B.7
- **source**: MAC-010
- **locator**: page 11
- **inclusive segments**: S00005–S00009

### D0005 — Gross international reserves remained adequate at 125% of ARA metric
- **actor**: Bank of Mexico (Banxico); Ministry of Finance
- **action**: reserves slightly declined from peak after the August 2021 SDR allocation of USD 12 billion; government bought USD 7 billion from central bank to meet public sector foreign currency debt amortization
- **mechanism**: asset-liability management
- **outcome**: reserves remained adequate at 125% of ARA metric coverage
- **dates**: post-August 2021; status through 2022
- **quantities**: USD 12 billion SDR allocation; USD 7 billion FX purchase; 125% ARA coverage
- **attribution**: IMF staff
- **period fit**: late 2021–2022
- **limitations**: institutional reserves; ruler attribution indirect
- **polarity**: positive (adequate reserves)
- **methodology IDs**: 5B.3, 5B.9
- **source**: MAC-010
- **locator**: page 11
- **inclusive segments**: S00009–S00012

### D0006 — Credit growth is recovering despite tighter financial conditions
- **actor**: Bank of Mexico data; financial sector
- **action**: loans to non-financial corporates began picking up late last year; FX loans reached nominal pre-pandemic levels; peso-denominated loans recovered after a year of stagnation; household loans picked up earlier, led by public non-bank mortgage lending
- **mechanism**: lagged transmission of monetary policy
- **outcome**: credit recovery underway; corporates entering tightening phase with healthy (but smaller than a decade ago) financial buffers
- **dates**: late 2021 through 2022 H1
- **quantities**: indexed to Dec 2019 = 100
- **attribution**: Haver Analytics; IMF staff
- **period fit**: 2021 late–2022 H1
- **limitations**: descriptive; ruler attribution indirect
- **polarity**: positive (functional credit channel)
- **methodology IDs**: 5B.6, 5B.9
- **source**: MAC-010
- **locator**: page 12
- **inclusive segments**: S00001–S00004

### D0007 — Banking system remained well-capitalized with profitability recovering
- **actor**: Mexican banking system
- **action**: maintained healthy balance sheets through the pandemic; total capital adequacy ratio increased to over 19 percent from 16 percent pre-pandemic; large institutions maintained ample liquidity buffers
- **mechanism**: regulatory capital and liquidity management
- **outcome**: well-capitalized system; profitability recovering
- **dates**: pre-pandemic to 2022 H1
- **quantities**: capital adequacy ratio >19% (vs 16% pre-pandemic)
- **attribution**: IMF staff
- **period fit**: 2019–2022 H1
- **limitations**: institutional/regulatory outcome; ruler attribution indirect
- **polarity**: positive (financial stability)
- **methodology IDs**: 5B.3, 5B.6
- **source**: MAC-010
- **locator**: page 12
- **inclusive segments**: S00005–S00007

### D0008 — Authorities smoothed retail fuel prices and stabilized food prices
- **actor**: Mexican authorities (executive and/or fiscal)
- **action**: smoothed retail fuel prices; fiscal cost of long-standing fuel pricing regime rose following Russian invasion of Ukraine, resulting in higher-than-budgeted subsidies in 2022 H1; secured a nonbinding agreement with several food producers and distributors to stabilize prices of 24 items for six months initially; provided a temporary tariff reduction on certain foods; took steps to reduce distribution costs and promote food production, especially by small farmers
- **mechanism**: price smoothing mechanism, voluntary producer agreement, tariff reduction, distribution-cost reduction
- **outcome**: stabilized (or attempted to stabilize) fuel and essential food prices; higher fiscal cost for fuel subsidies
- **dates**: 2022 H1
- **quantities**: 24 food items; six-month initial agreement
- **attribution**: IMF staff
- **period fit**: 2022 H1
- **limitations**: direct executive action; impact on inequality/incidence not quantified in passage
- **polarity**: positive (consumer protection; price stability support)
- **methodology IDs**: 5B.6, 5B.9, 6B.2, 6B.3, 8B.2, 8B.6
- **source**: MAC-010
- **locator**: page 12
- **inclusive segments**: S00008–S00010

### D0009 — PEMEX earnings more than doubled on higher oil prices
- **actor**: PEMEX (state oil company)
- **action**: reported earnings more than doubled to over USD 23 billion in H1 2022 vs same period prior year; modest increase in production
- **mechanism**: higher global oil prices
- **outcome**: improved cash generation; will mostly be used for debt amortization; PEMEX total debt outstanding has declined somewhat recently but remains high, including to suppliers; spreads on PEMEX external debt continue above Mexican government bonds and most oil sector peers
- **dates**: H1 2022
- **quantities**: USD 23 billion in H1 2022 earnings (EBITDA basis)
- **attribution**: IMF staff
- **period fit**: 2022 H1
- **limitations**: state-owned enterprise; ruler attribution indirect/structural
- **polarity**: mixed (positive cash flow; debt/risk concerns persist)
- **methodology IDs**: 5B.6, 5B.7
- **source**: MAC-010
- **locator**: page 12
- **inclusive segments**: S00013–S00014

### D0010 — Economic activity expected to slow in H2 2022 and 2023
- **actor**: IMF staff
- **action**: staff projects economic growth of 2.1 percent in 2022 and 1.2 percent in 2023
- **mechanism**: tighter global financial conditions, cooling U.S. growth, weakening domestic and U.S. demand
- **outcome**: employment growth slowing; current account balance expected to slightly widen to about 1 percent of GDP in 2022–23 as import prices increase faster than export prices
- **dates**: 2022 H2 onward; 2023; 2022–23
- **quantities**: 2.1% (2022); 1.2% (2023); ~1% of GDP current account
- **attribution**: IMF staff projections
- **period fit**: medium-term outlook
- **limitations**: forecast, not realized; ruler attribution indirect
- **polarity**: negative (deceleration)
- **methodology IDs**: 5B.7, 5B.9, 5B.10, 8B.7
- **source**: MAC-010
- **locator**: page 13
- **inclusive segments**: S00003–S00008

### D0011 — 2023 draft budget targets a small increase in overall deficit; fiscal stance about neutral
- **actor**: Mexican authorities (executive budget proposal)
- **action**: 2023 draft budget targets a small increase in overall deficit due to interest payments, 3.8 to 4.1 percent of GDP; staff estimates fiscal stance (based on change in structural primary balance) will be about neutral in 2023; expenditure in 2023 increased by 8.5 percent in nominal terms (or 0.1 pp of GDP) vs 2022 outturn; budget entails no change in tax code but highlights continued efforts to reduce tax evasion and avoidance
- **mechanism**: expenditure increase including higher interest payments, social pensions for elderly, priority infrastructure; raised funding for fertilizers, national milk procurement, rural supplies; expected excise improvement
- **outcome**: modest overall deficit; neutral fiscal stance; faster revenue expected from oil/excises
- **dates**: 2023 budget proposal
- **quantities**: deficit 3.8% (2022) → 4.1% (2023 draft); expenditure +8.5% nominal; structural primary balance near-neutral; GFS expenditure 28.0 (2022) → 28.2 (2023 draft); revenue 24.3 → 24.1
- **attribution**: IMF staff calculations; authorities' projection
- **period fit**: 2023 fiscal year
- **limitations**: draft, not enacted at time of report; ruler attribution direct (executive proposal)
- **polarity**: mixed (neutral stance; modest deficit, pro-poor spending)
- **methodology IDs**: 5B.1, 5B.3, 5B.6, 5B.8, 6B.3, 8B.1, 8B.2
- **source**: MAC-010
- **locator**: page 13
- **inclusive segments**: S00009–S00017

### D0012 — Inflation projected to plateau around 8½ percent in H2 2022 and decline gradually
- **actor**: IMF staff
- **action**: inflation projected to plateau at around 8½ percent in H2 2022 then decline gradually; core and headline inflation expected to return to midpoint of target band in mid-2024; assumes policy rate raised to around 10 percent by early 2023 and maintained before gradual reduction from late 2023
- **mechanism**: lagged monetary transmission; baseline forecast
- **outcome**: gradual disinflation path; risks to outlook tilted to the upside
- **dates**: H2 2022 plateau; mid-2024 return to target; early 2023 terminal rate; late 2023 cuts begin
- **quantities**: ~8.5% plateau; ~10% terminal rate
- **attribution**: IMF staff
- **period fit**: 2022 H2–2024
- **limitations**: forecast; ruler attribution indirect
- **polarity**: negative near-term (above-target inflation); upside risks
- **methodology IDs**: 5B.3, 5B.9, 8B.7
- **source**: MAC-010
- **locator**: page 14
- **inclusive segments**: S00001–S00003

### D0013 — Economic activity projected to pick up in 2024 with modest growth rebound, but no significant structural reforms
- **actor**: IMF staff
- **action**: economic activity projected to pick up in 2024 and following years, in tandem with the U.S.; output gap will narrow after widening somewhat in 2023; however, without significant structural reforms, the growth rebound is expected to be modest, to about 2 percent; potential output growth per capita would recover to a rate only slightly above one percent; current account deficit projected to stabilize at around 1 percent of GDP in the medium term
- **mechanism**: U.S. cycle, structural-reform gap
- **outcome**: modest medium-term growth; potential per-capita growth slipping
- **dates**: 2024 onward; medium term
- **quantities**: ~2% growth rebound; >1% per-capita potential; ~1% of GDP current account; population growth 0.7% per year 2022–27; potential GDP growth about 1.8% after 2024
- **attribution**: IMF staff
- **period fit**: 2024+ medium term
- **limitations**: forecast; "without significant structural reforms" is a conditional assumption; ruler attribution implicit
- **polarity**: negative (weak medium-term trajectory absent structural reform)
- **methodology IDs**: 5B.10, 8B.7, 8B.10
- **source**: MAC-010
- **locator**: page 14
- **inclusive segments**: S00003–S00006

### D0014 — Balance of risks to near-term growth tilted to the downside
- **actor**: IMF staff
- **action**: balance of risks to near-term outlook for economic growth tilted to the downside; main downside risks identified as higher global inflation and sharper global financial tightening, sharper deceleration in global or U.S. growth, additional external price shocks (including from Russia-Ukraine war), tighter-than-expected monetary policy leading to capital outflows, system-wide liquidity stress, peso depreciation, higher imported inflation, possibly exacerbated by remittance falls or competitiveness erosion; U.S. slowdown especially consequential given Mexican GDP elasticity above one with U.S.; on domestic side, slower-than-expected reversal of inflation surge if backward-looking price dynamics or rising inflation expectations; new COVID-19 variants with greater immune evasion could reduce mobility and raise precautionary saving
- **mechanism**: external and domestic channels
- **outcome**: downside risk skew
- **dates**: near-term (2022 H2–2023)
- **quantities**: Mexican GDP elasticity >1 with U.S.; illustrative peak output loss ≥2% in global inflation scenario
- **attribution**: IMF staff
- **period fit**: 2022 H2–2023
- **limitations**: risk assessment; ruler attribution indirect
- **polarity**: negative (downside risks dominate)
- **methodology IDs**: 5B.9, 5B.10, 8B.7, 8B.9
- **source**: MAC-010
- **locator**: page 14
- **inclusive segments**: S00007–S00015

### D0015 — Mexico's data adequacy for surveillance is generally adequate; national accounts high quality
- **actor**: IMF staff; INEGI (National Statistical Office)
- **action**: assessed data provision as adequate for surveillance; national accounts follow 2008 SNA recommendations; 2021 ROSC update found national accounts of high quality; significant improvements since 2015 in methodological and dissemination aspects; remaining areas for improvement include chained GDP volume indices with previous-period annual weights, treatment of goods for processing abroad, coverage of illegal activities, and accrual vs cash basis for some government transactions; CPI and PPI meet international standards; CPI reference period is second half of July 2018; PPI reference period is July 2019
- **mechanism**: statistical standards adherence
- **outcome**: high-quality national accounts; identified gaps
- **dates**: ROSC 2021; reference periods 2018 (CPI) and 2019 (PPI)
- **quantities**: PPI covers 79.2% of Mexican production
- **attribution**: IMF staff; 2021 Data ROSC
- **period fit**: 2021–2022
- **limitations**: descriptive; ruler attribution indirect
- **polarity**: positive (statistical capacity)
- **methodology IDs**: 5B.7, 8B.5
- **source**: MAC-010
- **locator**: page 100
- **inclusive segments**: S00001–S00014

### D0016 — Government finance statistics: comprehensive and timely except subnational; fiscal statistics aligned with GFSM2014
- **actor**: Mexican authorities (fiscal statistics compilers)
- **action**: fiscal statistics are comprehensive and timely except for the subnational sector; compile fiscal statistics following national concepts and aligned with GFSM2014; 2021 ROSC mission noted differences in classification and coverage make reconciliation between national and international presentations difficult; recommended publishing a table of all institutional units grouped by national presentation coverage, international presentation coverage, and GFSM2014 subsectors; full adoption of uniform accounting standards at subnational level would improve measure of public fixed investment in national accounts; pension liabilities partially reported; government securities reported at face value; official debt statistics exclude T-bonds issued to Banxico for liquidity management; federal government and Banxico accounting practices differ
- **mechanism**: statistical reporting framework
- **outcome**: identified gaps in subnational consolidation, pension debt reporting, T-bond treatment, and federal–central bank reconciliation
- **dates**: 2021 ROSC reference
- **quantities**: not quantified in passage
- **attribution**: IMF staff; 2021 Data ROSC
- **period fit**: 2021–2022
- **limitations**: descriptive; ruler attribution indirect
- **polarity**: mixed (adequate in national presentation; gaps at subnational level)
- **methodology IDs**: 5B.7, 5B.3, 8B.5
- **source**: MAC-010
- **locator**: page 100
- **inclusive segments**: S00015–S00018

### D0017 — Monetary/financial statistics methodology generally sound; FAS reporting; FSI reporting with gaps
- **actor**: Bank of Mexico; financial sector authorities
- **action**: methodological foundations of monetary statistics are generally sound; data on other financial intermediaries (insurance, pension funds) allow construction of financial corporation's survey with full coverage; Mexico reports data on some FAS indicators including gender-disaggregated financial-services use and two UN Target 8.10 indicators (commercial bank branches per 100,000 adults, ATMs per 100,000 adults); Mexico regularly reports monthly FSIs to IMF (14 core + 9 encouraged for deposit takers; 2 additional for OFCs; 1 additional for households; 1 additional for real estate); FSI reporting on non-financial corporate sector not reported; reporting temporarily interrupted after May 2021 to revise data per IFRS9, expected to resume by year end; authorities periodically produce updated FSIs in interim on old-standard basis on request
- **mechanism**: financial surveillance reporting
- **outcome**: sound monetary statistics; partial FSI reporting; non-financial corporate sector FSIs missing
- **dates**: through Oct 2022; FSI reporting pause after May 2021
- **quantities**: 14 core + 9 encouraged FSIs; 2 OFC FSIs; 1 household FSI; 1 real estate FSI
- **attribution**: IMF staff
- **period fit**: 2021–2022
- **limitations**: descriptive; ruler attribution indirect
- **polarity**: positive (sound) with gaps (non-financial corporate FSIs)
- **methodology IDs**: 5B.7, 8B.5
- **source**: MAC-010
- **locator**: page 101
- **inclusive segments**: S00005–S00012

### D0018 — External sector statistics are high quality; remaining BPM6/EDS issues
- **actor**: Bank of Mexico
- **action**: 2021 ROSC found external sector statistics of high quality; in 2017, Banxico migrated BOP and IIP to BPM6 (sixth edition); External Debt Statistics Guide 2013 not yet fully implemented; remaining issues include (i) intercompany external debt and SDR allocations in debt statistics; (ii) extending market valuation of liabilities to all financial institutions; (iii) recording public sector external debt interest on accrual basis; consistency could be improved between IIP and external debt; differences between BOP and national accounts in financial account transactions and positions; authorities participate in coordinated direct investment and portfolio investment surveys and disseminate reserve template and quarterly external debt statistics
- **mechanism**: standards migration and reporting
- **outcome**: high-quality ESS with identified gaps
- **dates**: 2017 BPM6 migration; 2021 ROSC reference
- **quantities**: not quantified in passage
- **attribution**: IMF staff; 2021 Data ROSC
- **period fit**: 2017–2022
- **limitations**: descriptive; ruler attribution indirect
- **polarity**: positive (high quality) with gaps
- **methodology IDs**: 5B.7, 8B.5
- **source**: MAC-010
- **locator**: page 101
- **inclusive segments**: S00012–S00019

### D0019 — Mexico subscribed to SDDS; latest SDDS Annual Observance Report and metadata available; ROSC updated December 2021
- **actor**: Mexico (as SDDS subscriber); IMF
- **action**: Mexico subscribed to the IMF's Special Data Dissemination Standard (SDDS) on August 13, 1996; latest SDDS Annual Observance Report and metadata available on the Dissemination Standards Bulletin Board; Mexico uses periodicity and timeliness flexibility options on central government debt and timeliness flexibility on general government operations; Mexico exceeds SDDS periodicity and timeliness requirements in many other data categories; updated data module ROSC was published in December 2021
- **mechanism**: international data standards subscription
- **outcome**: ongoing participation in data dissemination standards
- **dates**: August 13, 1996 (SDDS subscription); December 2021 (ROSC)
- **quantities**: not quantified
- **attribution**: IMF staff
- **period fit**: 1996–2022
- **limitations**: institutional; ruler attribution indirect
- **polarity**: positive (international standards adherence)
- **methodology IDs**: 5B.7, 8B.5
- **source**: MAC-010
- **locator**: page 102
- **inclusive segments**: S00001–S00004

### D0020 — Common surveillance indicators table lists current data availability, frequency, and quality assessments
- **actor**: Mexican authorities; IMF staff
- **action**: tabulated common indicators required for surveillance as of October 17, 2022; indicators include exchange rates (Oct 2022), international reserve assets (Oct 7, 2022), reserve/base money (Oct 7, 2022), broad money (Aug 2022), central bank balance sheet (Oct 7, 2022), consolidated banking system balance sheet (Aug 2022), interest rates (Oct 2022), CPI (Sep 30, 2022), general government revenue/expenditure (Aug 2022), central government revenue/expenditure (Aug 2022), central government debt (Aug 2022), external current account (Q2 2022), exports/imports (Aug 2022), GDP/GNP (Q2 2022), gross external debt (Q2 2022), IIP (Q2 2022); quality assessments combine data ROSC findings from 2010, 2012, and July 2021
- **mechanism**: data dissemination calendar
- **outcome**: current statistical reporting in place
- **dates**: October 17, 2022 (assessment date); various indicator dates
- **quantities**: table of 16+ indicators
- **attribution**: IMF staff
- **period fit**: as of October 2022
- **limitations**: descriptive; ruler attribution indirect
- **polarity**: positive (regular reporting)
- **methodology IDs**: 5B.7, 8B.5
- **source**: MAC-010
- **locator**: page 103
- **inclusive segments**: S00001–S00006

### D0021 — Common surveillance indicators table (concluded) covers external sector indicators
- **actor**: Mexican authorities; IMF staff
- **action**: continued indicators table for external current account balance (Q2 2022), exports/imports of goods and services (Aug 2022), GDP/GNP (Q2 2022), gross external debt (Q2 2022), IIP (Q2 2022); footnotes define reporting frequencies (D, W, M, Q, A, I, NA) and quality assessment methodology based on data ROSC conducted July 2021 (with consumer prices based on 2012 ROSC and monetary statistics on 2010 ROSC); quality assessment markings include O (fully observed), LO (largely observed), LNO (largely not observed), NO (not observed)
- **mechanism**: data dissemination calendar
- **outcome**: ongoing reporting
- **dates**: references Q2 2022 and Aug 2022 data
- **quantities**: not quantified
- **attribution**: IMF staff
- **period fit**: as of October 2022
- **limitations**: descriptive; ruler attribution indirect
- **polarity**: positive (regular reporting)
- **methodology IDs**: 5B.7, 8B.5
- **source**: MAC-010
- **locator**: page 104
- **inclusive segments**: S00001–S00012
